# Git Merge vs Git Rebase

## What They Do

**`git merge`** combines two branches by creating a new "merge commit" that has two parents, preserving the exact history of how development happened.

**`git rebase`** moves your commits to a new base, replaying them one by one on top of another branch, rewriting history to appear linear.

---

## Visual Comparison

**Starting point:**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \
feature:         D --- E
```

**After `git merge main` (on feature branch):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                \       \
feature:         D --- E --- M   ← merge commit (M has 2 parents)
```

**After `git rebase main` (on feature branch):**
```
main:    A --- B --- C
                         \
feature:                  D' --- E'   ← commits replayed, new hashes
```

---

## When to Use Each

### Use `git merge` when:
- Merging a **completed feature into main/develop** (the merge commit documents when it happened)
- Working on a **shared/public branch** others are using
- You want to **preserve exact history** — who branched when, from where
- Resolving conflicts **once** is preferable (merge handles it in one commit)

### Use `git rebase` when:
- **Updating your local feature branch** with upstream changes before a PR
- You want a **clean, linear history** that's easier to read
- Doing **interactive rebase** (`-i`) to clean up messy commits before sharing
- Working on a **private branch** no one else has checked out

---

## The Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves true history | Creates linear, cleaner history |
| Commits | Adds a merge commit | Rewrites commit SHAs |
| Conflicts | Resolved once | May need to resolve per-commit |
| Safety | Safe on shared branches | **Dangerous on shared branches** |
| Blame/bisect | Can be harder to follow | Easier to follow |
| Reversibility | Easy to undo | Harder to undo |

---

## The Golden Rule of Rebase

> **Never rebase a branch that others are working on.**

When you rebase, commits get new SHA hashes. If someone else has the old commits, their history diverges from yours and you'll create a mess when pushing.

```bash
# This will be rejected (or cause chaos if forced)
git rebase main
git push origin shared-branch  # ❌ Don't do this

# Force pushing after rebase is only safe on YOUR private branch
git push --force-with-lease origin my-feature-branch  # ✅ OK if truly private
```

---

## Common Workflows

**Keeping your feature branch up to date:**
```bash
git checkout feature-branch
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main        # Clean: replays your work on top of latest main
# vs
git merge origin/main         # Also works, but adds a merge commit
```

**Cleaning up commits before a PR:**
```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~4          # Interactively squash/reword last 4 commits
```

**Merging a finished feature:**
```bash
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature-branch   # --no-ff forces a merge commit even if fast-forward is possible
```

---

## Quick Decision Guide

```
Is the branch shared with others?
├── Yes → Use MERGE (always)
└── No (your private branch)
    ├── Want clean linear history? → REBASE
    ├── Cleaning up commits? → REBASE -i
    └── Don't care / want true history? → MERGE
```

---

## My Recommendation

A common pragmatic workflow:
1. **Rebase** your feature branch onto main while developing (keeps it current, clean history)
2. **Merge** (with `--no-ff`) into main when the feature is done (documents the integration point)

This gives you the benefits of both: clean feature branch history *and* a clear record of when features landed in main.
